  field by field, the graph made straight from the generator's in-memory models
  with the graph read back from the docs it writes (`index.json`). Over 14,336
  files on four workspaces there were 0 differences. The comparison can fail:
  one renamed symbol, one dropped edge and one removed file were all caught.

  So the trial's case is cost, not lost facts. The parser, the value slots' read
  side and the reversible escapes (about 900 of `document.ts`'s 1,253 lines),
  plus about 1,000 lines of tests, exist only so a written doc reads back as its
  model.

  Commit **78feba0e3** on the worktree's branch, on top of a1d580016. No product
  file was changed. The record is a dated probe, marked historical at its top:
  - `AI-Agent-Workspace/AgentSessionHistory/2026/11/2026-11-19/Probes/facts-with
  out-docs/README.md` (all seven parts)
  - `probe.cjs`: the comparison, plus an "analysis alone" mode that writes
  nothing. It wraps `renderLiveDoc` in the built CommonJS engine before the
  generator loads.
  - `time-inspect.sh`
  - `results/*.json`: small per-run results.

  The corpora were copied into a private folder, which I deleted afterwards. The
  cold folder was never written to.

  - **The two extra files** (`.vscode/settings.json`, `d3-force-3d.d.ts`) are

  and every corpus still finished.
  - **The model itself is already shaped by Markdown.** Its links are
  percent-encoded paths relative to where the doc would sit, and the graph
  decodes them again. Dropping the render, read-back and write alone frees
  nothing more; the links would have to become a file plus a symbol.
  - **A bug this hides:** `compose.ts:407` assumes the docs folder sits exactly
  two folders below the workspace.

  ## Part 3: costs
  High load throughout (about 21), so the time differences are rough.

  | Workspace | Full run: s, peak MB | Analysis alone: s, peak MB | Docs written
  | One graph file: pretty / compact / gzipped |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | This repository | 56.1, 485 | 56.1, 417 | 1,120, 4.3 MB | 9.45 / 6.75 / 1.16
  MB |
  | dbatools | 78.3, 492 | 68.7, 488 | 1,977, 4.0 MB, 9.3 MB on disk | 5.6 / 4.2
  / 0.67 MB |
  | tSQLt | 25.3, 310 | 24.6, 305 | 465, 1.2 MB | 2.3 / 1.6 / 0.13 MB |
  | DNN | 250.8, 1,566 | 202.5, 1,161 | 10,776, 22.8 MB text, 61.9 MB on disk |
  60.1 / 39.0 / 3.14 MB |

  - **Deriving the graph from the models** takes 0.03–1.1 s.
  - **`inspect`, one question on DNN:** 10.4–11.8 s today. Deriving the graph
  from the docs is 6.5–7.5 s of that; reading `index.json` instead would be
  1.4–1.9 s. With no stored graph it would mean re-analysing everything, 25–202
  s per question across the corpora.
  - **History:** from the history-rebuild-cost record's own numbers, with no new
  run, the docs' share is about 7–13 % of one commit's time. The cost sits in
  the index pass and the analysis, which removing the docs does not touch.

  ## Where this contradicts the brief or your recommendation
  1. **The count:** a1d580016 has 1,120 docs, not 1,093.
  2. **The skill is wrong:** `reference.md:49` says the command line and the
  Explorer read `index.json`. Both actually re-derive the graph from the docs.
  The only product reader of `index.json` is the history's
  `summarizeChange.ts:97`.
  3. **"Beside the board":** the estate reader already reads each scan's own
  folder (`graphFiles.ts:64–101`). Facts kept beside the board would make one
  scan's facts depend on which board names it, and a scan on two boards would be
  generated twice. I would keep them inside the scan, in a folder that ignores
  itself.
  4. **"Words as ordinary documents that link a file" loses something.** Today
  720 links from authored words to 158 documents count as the file's relations.
  Moved into separate documents, those become document-to-document links, which
  the graph does not carry. The history would also lose them, because its
  sequence carries only the forward links.

     If every doc became a citing document, the bundle would go from 158 to
  1,278 documents. The 3D documentation overlay would gain 1,120 nodes, each
  tied to one file, and Knowledge Sources could not tell a file's own words from
  a design document.
  5. **Without docs the stored graph is a cache.** That reverses the 2026-09-28
  reason "it is not a cache", and should be put to the owner as a reversal.

  ## Forks, with my choice for each
  - **Where the facts live:** inside the scanned folder, in a folder that
  ignores itself. Commit nothing derived.
  - **How a consumer knows they are fresh:** the stored graph carries a
  fingerprint (the generator identity the history already computes, the
  configuration, and a listing of the discovered files). On a mismatch, say
  "stale" and regenerate. The per-file store of the 2026-10-19 decision stays
  the later work; the fingerprint check is what its resolution step would run
  first anyway.
  - **The commands and checks:**
    - `generate` writes the stored graph, and `--check` becomes the fingerprint
  check. Drop `--include` and `--changed` until the per-file store exists.
    - `lint` keeps only its structural checks over the graph.
    - `find-orphans` is deleted.
    - The gate's "Live Docs" stage and CI become "generate, then lint".
    - Pages generates before building.
    - The history's check at the head compares against a fresh generation, and
  should say plainly what it no longer checks.
  - **The export:** a one-way, on-demand Markdown export, never read back. The
  Explorer's download already does exactly this.
  - **A file's own top comment:** one general reader by comment syntax as the
  floor, with each language's own reader overriding it where one exists. In the
  model, call it `description`, not "opening", which already means a route or
  procedure.
  - **What the agent skill reads:** `inspect --json`, plus one new "everything
  about this file" question.
  - **New fork: where a file's own words live.** One words document per file at
  a path convention. In this repository that is the same path, words only, so
  the 8,724 existing links to those paths (from 173 documents) and the history
  keep working. Its links count as the file's.

  ## The road
  Seven steps; each leaves a working product and a green gate.
  1. The generator returns the graph it made, and the history takes it instead
  of reading `index.json`.
  2. Read each file's top comment into the model.
  3. Consumers read the stored graph with its fingerprint.
  4. Move the words into their own documents.
  5. Stop writing per-file docs; deletes the parser and the round-trip tests.
  6. Links in the model become a file plus a symbol.
  7. Add the export command.

  Every step except 7 changes code the history's cache is keyed on. I would land
  1–3 in one rebuild and 4–6 in a second.

  - The cost of the fingerprint check itself (a discovery walk plus `git
  ls-files -s` on DNN) is the next thing I would measure.

❯ What I think any format must do here, whatever its speed. Correct me if any

  a

  Here is what I'll say as a rule of thumb about these lists of requirements in
  general:
  - You are listing off important values that we care about maximizing
  - Reality will likely push back against us and force us to be unable to
  maximize all of our values simultaneously
  - Dimensionality reduction algorithms fit high-dimensional data wildly more
  efficiently by allowing a little bit of nudge in the axes off-orthogonal.

  What you will likely find as you try to maximize the things you care about
  and minimize the ones you don't is that you land on a handful of quite
  radically different solutions with substantial tradeoffs, forcing bends in
  certain rules or constraints to accommodate something that is often even
  better than what we had originally envisioned. Nudge dimensions and
  requirements to permute the idea space and find those actual interesting
  local minima that we would think of as logical-endpoint ideas along various
  logical experiment trajectories.

● That changes how I'll brief the format research, and I've written your rule
  into owner.md so it carries into later design work.

  I had framed those four points as tests a candidate passes or fails. I'll
  treat them as four values instead: relax each one in turn and follow where it
  leads. The research then brings back a handful of designs that differ in kind,
  each with what it bends, what it buys and the measurements, rather than one
  ranked list of survivors.

  What each bend opens up:

  - Bend "the page reads the store itself": the tools keep one form built for
    questions, and the page is shipped a different form built for drawing.
  - Bend "nothing installed, nothing compiled": a real database engine, with
    queries that never read the whole file.
  - Bend "the same bytes for the same facts": container formats such as HDF5
    that do not write byte-identical files; runs would be compared by content
    instead.
  - Bend "one file": a folder of small pieces fetched as needed. The history's
    words are already stored that way, in 500 parts.

  Where a design bends something you gave as fixed, such as your work machine's
  limits or the page's no-network rule, I'll name the bend so the choice is
  yours.

  lines I read.

  The durations in your screenshot include waiting. #275 shows 1 h 18 m, but 76
  minutes of that was queueing behind #274. The workflow runs one at a time and
  keeps only the newest waiting push, which is what you had assumed.

  Pushing less often would save very little. A push that changes no engine code
  costs about two minutes. The minutes are in the full history rebuilds on
  GitHub's machine: 279 of the 882 came from those three runs.

  - #274 was waste. The cache key at the time included package.json, so an
    unrelated change threw the cache away. That was fixed on November 19: the
    history command now decides what can be reused.
  - #276 and #277 were real. Each engine landing that reaches main costs one
    rebuild there, however many commits or pushes carry it. It is the same
    rebuild I ran here tonight, and tonight's landing made it lighter: 50
    minutes instead of two hours.

  What's coming: two or three more engine landings (the readers, then the store
  change in two steps), so about 50 minutes each, once.

  I would change neither the workflow nor the branches. As far as I know GitHub
  doesn't bill standard-runner minutes on a public repository, so the cost is
  the wait and not money; your billing page will confirm that.

  The browser cases are past 590 with 4 failure marks so far. I'll run those
  down when the stage ends, before calling the landing ready.

  I committed `2c569bfb6` on `worktree-agent-a0dee84f8896c6bcc`, on top of

  The record is `AI-Agent-Workspace/AgentSessionHistory/2026/11/2026-11-19/Probe
  s/landing-reds/README.md`. It holds every measurement and five pictures, each
  described. It also has a per-case summary with the next step.

  **How I told code from data.** The landing changed the stored doc format, so
  today's builder can't read the old docs. I built the old data with the old
  builder from a `git archive` of `3d2bdc683` into scratch. Then I swapped
  `explorer-data.json` under today's client. All three cases pass on the old
  data and fail on today's: case 1 and case 2 each ran once each way, case 3
  went 8 of 8 green on old and 0 of 8 on new. All three reds come from the map's
  growth, not from the landing's code.

  **Case 1, `local-map-directories.spec.ts` (now line 558).**
  - **What it protects:** freeing the width makes an opened directory stand
  wider, and the link carries that choice to another screen.
  - **Cause:** `scripts/live-docs` gained five files.
    - At the default Width Cost, the shapes priced were no wrap 72,209, 12 rows
  42,023, 6 rows 39,353 (chosen) and 4 rows 42,843.
    - At Width Cost 0 they were 69,049, 37,033, 32,533 (6 rows, chosen again)
  and 34,193.
    - The price's walk stops at the first shape that isn't cheaper, so the lever
  lowers the price but no longer changes the choice. On the old data it went
  from 4 rows to 2.
  - **Is the product right:** yes. It follows the walk's documented rule, and
  today's picture at the default is a sound four-column picture. Whether 2 rows
  would be cheaper today is unknown, because the walk never tries it.
  - **What I changed:** the case now opens the estate sample's `Contracts`, a
  fixed program. It stands narrow at the default (3 columns, 1,002 px) and in 2
  rows at Width Cost 0 (4 columns, 1,374 px).
  - **Proof it can still fail:** I made the shape's price ignore the lever (a
  temporary change, removed and rebuilt). The case went red at `free.shape not
  equal`.
  - **Now:** green 5 of 5.

  **Case 2, `return-cost.spec.ts` (now line 87).**
  - **What it protects:** the Return Cost a link names is the one the search
  prices with, and Tuning shows it.
  - **Cause:** the landing made the manifest and its adapters read through
  `tooling/sourceText.ts`. With that card in the picture, the order with no
  return is cheaper in wire alone. The search adopts it at every Return Cost, 0
  included; on the old data it kept the greedy order at 500 and adopted at
  1,000.
  - **Is the product right:** yes. Today's picture at 500 puts every adapter in
  one column with no return, and it reads well. There is simply no trade left
  there for the lever to decide.
  - **What I changed:** the link's case now uses the Rosetta C# pair
  `Models/ModelFactory.cs` and `Models/Record.cs`. The greedy order shows 2
  returns; the other order shows 1 and costs 1,786 px more wire. A link naming
  500 keeps the greedy order (`[2]`, one trial), a link naming 4,000 adopts the
  other (`[2, 1]`), and Tuning shows each value. The case no longer depends on
  where the default sits.
  - **Proof it can still fail:** I made the search ignore the link's cost. The
  case went red at "at 4,000 px a return is worth the wire".
  - **Now:** green 5 of 5. The two spec files together passed whole, 17 cases.
  The other two cases in this file still use the manifest and pass, but they
  could drift the same way later.

  **Case 3, `force-graph-focus.spec.ts` (now line 182).**
  - **What it protects:** a focused link centres its file, a click on its sphere
  pins it, More opens its details, and Centre on brings it back to the centre.
  - **This contradicts the brief:** on a quiet machine it is not intermittent.
  It failed 8 of 8 at one worker and 10 of 12 at two workers, in three ways:
    - **Turn fails** (1 of 8): the camera turned 0°.
    - **Click misses** (3 of 8): the click did not pin `graph.ts`.
    - **Centre off** (4 of 8): after Centre on, `graph.ts` sat 30 to 46 px from
  the centre.
  - **Cause of the first two, shown:** the page gives a press to the nearest
  sphere or wrapper skin, and a directory shell is drawn as its skin alone. The
  helpers only checked sphere discs. So a turn could start on a shell's skin and
  grab it (camera 0°), and a click could land on the translucent `explorer`
  shell standing in front of `graph.ts`.
  - **What I changed:** a new helper, `pressedAt`, computes what a press would
  take, from the drawn buffers: spheres at their drawn centre and radius, skins
  as their uploaded triangles, skins opening skipped.
    - A background point must take nothing at both ends of the drag and 8 px
  around each.
    - The click point must take `graph.ts` itself.
    - If no point of the frame qualifies, it throws a plain error. There is no
  retry and no longer timeout.
  - **Result after the mend:** 13 runs, with no failure at the turn or the
  click.
  - **Still failing:** every run fails after Centre on (5 of 5 in the last run),
  at line 198. The picture is still (`aria-busy` false, substeps unchanged) and
  the camera stops within half a second. `graph.ts` then rests 14 to 46 px left
  of the room's centre and 2 to 4 px low, steady for six seconds, and the
  offset differs from run to run.
  - **Ruled out:**
    - A turn alone does not cause it: on the old data with one forced turn, 6 of
  6 passed.
    - The detail panel was closed when the framing ran.
  - **Cause: not found**, so I can't yet say whether the page or the case is
  wrong.
  - **Next step:** in a scratch build, log frame by frame after Centre on the
  framing's own `target`, `insets` and the camera's orientation in
  `forceGraphView.ts`. Also repeat the pin and Centre on with the old data, to
  tell the picture from the code.

  **Undone:**
  - `npm run live-docs:generate` ran before I edited the authored notes and
  showed 0 docs changed. I did not run it again after those edits.
  `live-docs:lint` and the markdown link check are clean.
  - `safe:commit` was not run, since I touched nothing outside `tests/e2e`, the
  Live Docs' authored notes and the record. ESLint on the three specs is clean.
  - These are stale but outside my files:
    - the `nominalMeasurer` comment in `directory-flow.ts` about

    - the decisions log's "`manifest.ts` at 1175".

  **Slip-ups:**
  - My scratchpad already held a folder `old` left by the November 19 round. A

❯ >Undo. Back walks through every act; or a second history for acts beside Back
  (my recommendation, pins first); or only destructive acts become Back steps.

  - Pros: you don't have to click back a ton to go back to the website you were
  previously at (I just experienced this going from github to the hosted
  github pages explorer)
  - Cons: your current URL is no longer the basic shareable unit. Link
  generation becomes more independent of present URL. Bookmarking does not
  return a user to the state they bookmarked.

  >A click on a pinned 3D sphere unpins it and replaces the picture. Five of
  six blind testers did that first. Should it?

  Probably not. We probably need to go back to the UX drawing board and be
  holistic with respect to "Open/Close" and "Pin" states. We talked about this
  fairly extensively on the 11/18 dev day chat.

  >SQL system catalog names (sys, INFORMATION_SCHEMA) no longer drawn as
  connections. This revises your word of October 9; I recommend it.

  That's fine if you wish to no longer draw them as connections. Balance the
  potentially-competing concerns of:
  - Simplicity of the resultant codebase/architecture
  - Aesthetics of the typical view
  - Strong correctness guarantees (no false positives or false negatives in a
  scan)

  >The linked server. Which board piece carries the line saying what its name
  stands for: the SQL Server piece or the Oracle piece?

  That is a great question. I would generally suspect the SQL Server piece?

  >Documents as nodes. Three things are open: whether a document with no links
  in or out is drawn, how a document looks in 2D, and what one switch keeps
  out.

  This and "Assets" should haunt you a bit. (Indeed, perhaps a Document is an
  "Asset"-archetyped node which is capable of carrying symbols (markdown
  headers). Because we're going to run into situations where these objects --
  "Assets" -- vastly outnumber non-asset files. And what we'll want to be
  thinking about what we want to do when we encounter those and similar
  situations. (And whether the emergent render is just fine without worrying
  too much about it).

  Should documents which have no references be nodes?

  Should other source control-tracked scanned files be ignored in general? I
  guess we ignore packages folders in scans but isn't that also a function of
  the gitignore? I guess what I mean to say is: why should the scan ignore them
  if git won't? Should it be optional/configurable? Yes! Folks should be able
  to configure what file formats and paths they scan and... well, we indeed
  have such configuration, no?

  >The old history cache (251 MB, its comparison done): remove it?

  Clean up as needed. Remove it.

  >Every picture file gets a doc (a fifth of one test codebase's docs). Your
  rule of October 15 says yes; confirm or narrow.

  (Or gets an entry of some sort in whatever datastore exists to represent
  things which have been scanned)

  >December. What may leave the work machine; roughly how much code, and git or
  TFS; which shapes it has most of (scripts calling each other's functions,
  scripts running SQL, user controls, procedures named from C#). Public
  repositories that resemble it are welcome.

  I will look into that and see if I can find some public repos which resemble
  what we have. That's a good idea.

❯ >Undo. Back walks through every act; or a second history for acts beside Back
  (my recommendation, pins first); or only destructive acts become Back steps.

  - Pros: you don't have to click back a ton to go back to the website you were
  previously at (I just experienced this going from github to the hosted
  github pages explorer)
  - Cons: your current URL is no longer the basic shareable unit. Link
  generation becomes more independent of present URL. Bookmarking does not
  return a user to the state they bookmarked.

  >A click on a pinned 3D sphere unpins it and replaces the picture. Five of
  six blind testers did that first. Should it?

  Probably not. We probably need to go back to the UX drawing board and be
  holistic with respect to "Open/Close" and "Pin" states. We talked about this
  fairly extensively on the 11/18 dev day chat.

  >SQL system catalog names (sys, INFORMATION_SCHEMA) no longer drawn as
  connections. This revises your word of October 9; I recommend it.

  That's fine if you wish to no longer draw them as connections. Balance the
  potentially-competing concerns of:
  - Simplicity of the resultant codebase/architecture
  - Aesthetics of the typical view
  - Strong correctness guarantees (no false positives or false negatives in a
  scan)

  >The linked server. Which board piece carries the line saying what its name
  stands for: the SQL Server piece or the Oracle piece?

  That is a great question. I would generally suspect the SQL Server piece?

  >Documents as nodes. Three things are open: whether a document with no links
  in or out is drawn, how a document looks in 2D, and what one switch keeps
  out.

  This and "Assets" should haunt you a bit. (Indeed, perhaps a Document is an
  "Asset"-archetyped node which is capable of carrying symbols (markdown
  headers). Because we're going to run into situations where these objects --
  "Assets" -- vastly outnumber non-asset files. And what we'll want to be
  thinking about what we want to do when we encounter those and similar
  situations. (And whether the emergent render is just fine without worrying
  too much about it).

  Should documents which have no references be nodes?

  Should other source control-tracked scanned files be ignored in general? I
  guess we ignore packages folders in scans but isn't that also a function of
  the gitignore? I guess what I mean to say is: why should the scan ignore them
  if git won't? Should it be optional/configurable? Yes! Folks should be able
  to configure what file formats and paths they scan and... well, we indeed
  have such configuration, no?

  >The old history cache (251 MB, its comparison done): remove it?

  Clean up as needed. Remove it.

  >Every picture file gets a doc (a fifth of one test codebase's docs). Your
  rule of October 15 says yes; confirm or narrow.

  things which have been scanned)

● Thanks. Here is what each answer changed, with one correction (undo) and
  answers to the two questions you asked back.

  Done or settled

  - Old history cache: removed (280 MB on disk).
  - SQL catalog names: the change stays on the SQL reader's branch and lands
    with the readers. On your three concerns:
    - Simplicity: it is a short fixed list in the SQL reader (two schemas, three
      built-in functions).
    - The view: on the test codebase, 207 of the 213 names still wrongly kept as
      loose ends were these.
    - Correctness: in SQL Server no object of yours can live in those schemas,
      so no connection between scanned things is lost. What is given up is the
      fact that a script reads the catalog at all.
  - Linked server: the SQL Server piece, as you suspected. That is also where
    the name lives: it is an entry in the SQL Server instance's own
    configuration, and Oracle knows nothing of it.
  - Pictures: taken as "every scanned file has an entry in the store". Whether
    that entry is a Markdown doc stops mattering once the store changes.
  - December: noted. Any repositories you find become standing test subjects.

  Undo: the cons don't follow

  Every pin today already rewrites the address in place without adding a Back
  step; that is why Back skips pins. An undo history would work the same way:
  undo restores the earlier state and rewrites the address to match. So under
  all three designs the address names what is on screen, a copied link carries
  it, and a bookmark returns to it. A link would not carry the list of past
  states, but the browser's own history is not in a link either.

  Your pro is real, and it points at something I had not offered. The Back
  presses you needed to return to GitHub are today's behaviour: every move to
  another file, view or folder adds one. A second history stops pins from adding
  more, but does not reduce those. Reducing them means the page keeps its own
  history for places too, behind its own back arrow, so the browser's Back
  leaves in one press. The cost is that the browser's Back, Alt+← and the
  mouse's side button stop stepping within the Explorer. I'll bring that as an
  alternative inside the design below, since undo is part of the same question.

  Open, close and pin: back to the drawing board

  I re-read what the record holds before designing anything:

  │ agreed)                │     │ button.                                  │
  ├────────────────────────┼─────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤

  On November 18 we found three strengths of holding already in the product,
  unnamed: the preview (3D's "discovery"), open (an opened folder or popped
  bubble), and pinned. We also found that nothing lets go, and you approved Fold
  others away and Unpin others.

  So the same click means "look" in 2D and "pin or unpin" in 3D. In 3D the
  strongest hold is the one a stray click removes, which is what cost five of
  six strangers their picture.

  What I'll bring: two or three whole models, each a small table of what a
  click, a second click, the pin button and × do to a thing in each state, the
  same in both maps, with undo's place in each. Then trials you can try behind a
  lever, with strangers' readings.

  One candidate, to show the kind of thing. It is the editor's model you raised
  on November 18:
  - A click opens a thing, so it joins the picture.
  - A click on something already open or pinned only selects it.
  - The pin button makes it durable.
  - Only ×, Fold others away or Unpin others lets go.

  Your November 2 wish, that a second click takes back the first, would then be
  met by undo, not by the click itself.

  Documents, assets, and what the scan leaves out

  - Yes, the configuration exists. glob chooses which files are scanned (every
    file by default) and exclude names paths to skip. Git's ignore rules decide
    the rest: what git ignores is left out, and a tracked file is never ignored.
  - But five fixed rules skip files whatever you configure: .git, node_modules
    at any depth, the folder the docs are written to, lock files, and documents
    (the October 22 "no doc for a doc" rule). By your principle, the last four
    should be defaults a configuration can change. I'll make that part of the
    store's change, where the documents rule and the docs-folder rule fall away
    anyway.
  - Should a document nothing links be a node? My recommendation: it gets an
    entry like every scanned file, and the maps treat it as they treat any other
    file that connects to nothing. The 3D map already has that case (the
    islands, which "Next step" leaves out), so documents need no rule of their
    own.
  - A document as an asset that carries symbols. I'd put it this way: every file
    is a node, and whether it offers symbols depends only on whether a reader
    exists for its format (headings for Markdown, nothing for a PNG). Kind is
    then only a colour and a switch. That makes a document and a picture the
    same sort of node, as you suggest, without changing your October 16 rule
    that an asset is a binary file.
  - Assets outnumbering code: I'd rather look than guess. Show Assets is off by
    default, so the first picture would not change; the question is what happens
    with it on. I'll add a public repository where pictures or documents far
    outnumber code to the standing run and bring you its pictures in every view,
    with the scan's time and size.

● The first of tonight's measurements is in and reviewed: where the browser

  What it found

  - The stage took 43 minutes for 609 cases: 596 passed, 6 failed, 7 skipped by
    design. Two of the six are real. One is the known long 3D settle that waits
    on your eye for Settle Hold. The other is a second focus case that fails
    about one run in three; I've passed it to the focus builder. The other four
    were the builder's own set-up.
  - Loading the page is not the main cost. A load and its first picture is about
    a fifth of the time. The rest is the cases acting on the page and waiting
    for it.
  - A tenth of the time is fixed pauses. The suite sleeps 1,089 times for a set
    number of milliseconds, 462 seconds in all, often right after it has already
    waited for the picture to come to rest.
  - A 3D picture takes 5 to 7 seconds to settle whatever the map's size. The
    physics takes one step per drawn frame, about 300 frames, while the
    processor sits 40% idle on the small sample.
  - The 2D page's first picture takes 1.8 seconds on this repository. About a
    third of that is the browser recomputing layout because our code measures a
    card, writes, then measures the next.
  - Your alarms are few. Of 636 time limits in the suite, 11 are bounds that
    mean "the product is too slow". The rest are plain waits.

  What I'll build from it

  All of it comes after the Playwright fix lands, since each is proved in a
  browser.

  1. Pauses become waits for the event, in tests only, each case shown still
     able to fail. About 2 minutes off the stage.
  2. The 2D map measures every card first, then writes, with pictures identical
     to the byte. About 0.3 s off every 2D render of this repository, for users
     too.
  3. The layout search draws connections only for a picture it adopts, not for
     every one it tries. Users always have the search on.

  One fork for you, to sit beside Settle Hold

  The physics could take more than one step in a frame that has time to spare.
  The picture would reach the same rest in fewer frames, roughly halving a 3D
  settle, and the motion you see would run faster. That changes how the map
  feels, so it is yours to choose; I'll bring it as a lever you can try.

  ## The `force-graph-focus` case: the camera was right; the page hid the file's
  name, and the case read where that hidden name had last stood

  **What the page aims at and where it ends.** I added temporary logging to the
  3D view and wrote a probe case (neither committed). In six runs on `21b6e602`
  they recorded every frame after the press of Centre on.
  - **The framing aims correctly.** It aims at `graph.ts` in the room the
  controls leave (right inset 0 and bottom inset 64 once the reader has closed).
  Its last frame, at 650 ms, puts the drawn sphere at (509.5, 303.0) in a 1,019
  × 606 room. That is the room's centre to 0.1 px, in all six runs, with the
  picture still.
  - **Then the page hides the file's name.** It happens as the sphere comes to
  rest: at 972 ms in one run (the name then at 509.1, 303.0), and at 797 ms in
  two others (486.0, 305.5 and 479.0, 306.1). Those last two are 23.5 and 30.5
  px left and 2.5 and 3.1 px low. A hidden name keeps its last `style.left/top`.
  - **The case read that stale place.** It checked `toBeVisible` once,
  mid-flight, and then polled the position. So the "14 to 46 px off, a different
  offset each run" was wherever the flight happened to be when the name was
  hidden.
  - **Why the name was hidden.** The file's own actions (Pin, Centre, More) held
  keyboard focus on More the whole time. The case presses More, then Inspect;
  the menu returns focus to More, and the reader returns it to More again when
  its own Centre on closes it. The strip was then frozen on screen by
  `positionActionStrip`: "a settling sphere must not pull a control away from a
  person aiming at it or using the keyboard". So it stayed where More had been
  pressed, above `graph.ts`'s position then, at (459–573, 267–309) in the frame,
  just below the room's centre. Centre on brought the file back under it. Every
  side the name could take collided with the strip, so the page hid the name,
  and the strip covered the file.
  - **Why the old map passed.** On the map before the engine round (1,093 files)
  no turn was needed and `graph.ts` was clicked at the centre itself. The strip
  stood above the centre and the name had room below it.

  **Verdict:** the case and the page were both wrong, and the root cause was in
  the page. The case read the stale place of a hidden name. The page left the
  subject's own strip over it, which hid its name; that goes against the strip's
  own documented purpose ("keep the accessible controls with the sphere while
  the simulation or camera moves").

  **`:182`, your question.** It is the same case, not a different fault. At
  `21b6e602`, line 182 of `force-graph-focus.spec.ts` is "a focused URL centers
  its node, direct clicks pin it, and More opens its details". It was `:108` at
  `16629d43`, and the helpers added in `89f6d813` pushed it down. Failing 1 of 3
  alone fits what I measured: the case only fails when the name is hidden more
  than 8 px from the centre. On my branch it is now `:131` and passed 10 of 10
  alone at one worker, which is the run of ten you asked for.

● The focus case is explained, and its fix is one review pass from landing.

  The camera was right all along. After "Centre on", the builder's
  frame-by-frame logging puts graph.ts at the room's centre to a tenth of a
  pixel in all six runs. The 14 to 46 px "off centre" was the test reading the
  last position of a name the page had hidden.

  The real fault was in the page. The file's own three buttons (Pin, Centre,
  More) covered it:
  - Reading a file through More gives keyboard focus back to More when the
    reader closes.
  - Since October 20, buttons holding keyboard focus were made to stand still on
    the screen.
  - So the camera flew the file to the centre and left its buttons behind, right
    where the file came to rest, and the name had nowhere to go.

  Before and after: the file under its own buttons, unnamed (.claude/worktrees/a
  gent-a355833c53ded4750/AI-Agent-Workspace/AgentSessionHistory/2026/11/2026-11-
  19/Probes/landing-reds/focus-before-name-hidden-under-its-actions.png) and
  buttons above, name below (.claude/worktrees/agent-a355833c53ded4750/AI-Agent-
  Workspace/AgentSessionHistory/2026/11/2026-11-19/Probes/landing-reds/focus-aft
  er-centre-named-beside-its-actions.png). I looked at both; the second reads
  well. They are still on the builder's branch.

  By the builder's account the case now passes 10 of 10 alone and the 3D family
  80 of 81; the one red is the known long settle that waits on Settle Hold. It
  also turns red again when the fix is undone. I have not rerun it myself. The
  second focus failure the suite builder saw is this same case at a different
  line number.

  The one change I asked for. The builder kept half of the old rule: buttons
  holding keyboard focus stay where their sphere stood while the sphere moves
  on. That still detaches them in the commonest 3D flow: press Pin with the
  mouse, move the pointer away, and the picture grows and carries the sphere
  off. I asked for the simpler rule: the buttons go with the thing they act on,
  except under the pointer or an open menu. I found no recorded reason for the
  keyboard half of the old rule. The builder is to say so if it knows one, and
  otherwise to write the new rule into the design system in the same commit.

  Left alone on purpose: if you press the buttons' own Centre with the mouse,
  they stay under your pointer while the file flies off. That belongs to the
  open/close/pin design.

  ## What I found

  1. **The install hang is fixed, as you expected.** I ran `npx playwright
  install chromium` on Node 26.13.1 in a lane hold, into
  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/tmp/claude-1000/pwup/browsers`. It finished in **39
  s**, downloads included, at load 5.4. It installed:
     - Chrome for Testing 159.0.8154.6 (`chromium-1255`)
     - Chrome Headless Shell 159.0.8154.6 (`chromium_headless_shell-1255`)
     - FFmpeg (`ffmpeg-1013`)

     I did not touch the default folder or any process I did not start.

     Cause, confirmed in the installed code:
     - 1.58.2 unpacks through `zipBundle.extract`
  (`playwright-core/lib/server/registry/oopDownloadBrowserMain.js`), which
  bundles `yauzl@3.2.0`.
     - 1.65.1 bundles `yauzl@3.4.0`. yauzl's 3.3.1 notes list fixes for
  "interrupting streams with `destroy()` and with async iteration on read
  streams".
     - I read issue 40724 itself. The hang is in extraction, the reporter blames
  yauzl (thejoshwolfe/yauzl#168), and it was closed by Playwright's PR 40747 on
  2026-05-09.
     - The issue does not name the release that fixed it. Users' commits on it
  name 1.60.0.
     - I did not find the exact yauzl line that ends the stall.

  2. **The whole stage could not run on 1.65.1.** Build (20 s) and bundles (45
  s, with the main checkout's history copied in, 1,333 commits) each had their
  own lane hold. The stage started at 06:00 and stopped after 11 s on the
  suite's own guard in `renderer-report.ts`: `WebGL in this run is drawn by:
  ANGLE (Google, Vulkan 1.3.0 (SwiftShader Device (Subzero) (0x0000C0DE)),
  SwiftShader driver)`. No case ran, so there is no case-by-case comparison yet.

     Mesa's EGL was installed system-wide by then (`libegl1 1.7.0-1+b2`,
  `libegl-mesa0 25.0.7-2+deb13u1`, `libgl1-mesa-dri`, `d3d12_dri.so` present).
  The private copies I fetched went unused.

  3. **The cause is the new Chromium, not the machine.** I wrote a probe
  (`gpu-probe.ts`) that launches a browser exactly as the suite does, using
  `browserLaunchOptions()` unchanged. Same machine, same Playwright 1.65.1, same
  flags:

     | Headless shell | Renderer |
     | --- | --- |
     | 145.0.7632.6 (1.58.2's; the focus builder's copy, only read) | `ANGLE
  (Microsoft Corporation, D3D12 (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090), OpenGL ES 3.1)` |
     | 159.0.8154.6 (1.65.1's) | SwiftShader |

     On 159 these all still gave SwiftShader:
     - adding `--ignore-gpu-blocklist`
     - adding `--use-gl=angle`
     - both together
     - the full Chrome for Testing 159 in new headless mode

     With `--enable-logging=stderr --v=1`, 159's GPU process says why it gives
  up; 145 logs none of these lines:
     ```
     ERROR:ui/gl/gl_surface_egl.cc:267] No suitable EGL configs found.
     ERROR:ui/gl/gl_surface_egl.cc:1013] No suitable EGL configs found for
  initialization.
     ERROR:gpu/ipc/service/gpu_init.cc:124] CollectGraphicsInfo failed.
     ERROR:components/viz/service/main/viz_main_impl.cc:192] Exiting GPU process
  due to errors during initialization
     ```
     So Chromium somewhere between 145 and 159 asks Mesa's EGL, through the
  `--use-angle=gl-egl` path, for a configuration Mesa's `d3d12` driver does not
  offer, then falls back to software without a word.

  ## Release notes, 1.59 to 1.65 (read through playwright.dev, not run)

  None mentions the headless shell against new headless mode, launch arguments,
  GPU, WebGL, ANGLE, SwiftShader, `page.clock`, `expect.poll` defaults,
  `webServer` or `globalSetup`.

  Items that could matter to this suite once it runs:
  - **1.65:** actions wait for elements to stop being inert, and fail on a
  timeout if they stay inert. The Explorer sets `inert` in `dom.ts`,
  `detailPanel.ts`, `errors.ts` and `index.ts`.

  `window.screen`.

  clipboard.

  working.

  reads as empty.
  - I did not use glob's `ignore` object, because glob takes either patterns or
  the object, not both. The walkers already pass patterns, so the object would
  mean rebuilding glob's matcher with its private defaults (case rule, root of
  patterns that begin with `/`).
  - Escaping folder names into patterns would not survive brace expansion.
  - If a later glob stopped calling the fs functions, the folders would simply
  be walked again and no file would be lost.

  ### What git does, from experiments (git 2.56.1)
  - Folders: a folder an excludes pattern names (or whose every entry is
  ignored) is listed once with a slash. Git descends into an ignored folder that
  holds a tracked file. It never descends into a nested repo. A worktree or
  nested repo inside an ignored folder is covered by that folder's entry. From a
  subfolder the paths are relative; from an ignored folder git prints `./`.
  - `--no-empty-directory` also drops single ignored files inside untracked,
  unignored folders. That is irrelevant here, since only slash entries are read.
  - `git check-ignore` refuses the whole call (exit 128) for any one path that
  is in a submodule, passes through a link to a folder, or starts with a `:` it
  reads as pathspec magic (`:(bogus)`, `:!`). A `:` later in the path is
  answered normally.
  - Glob follows no link under a leading `**`. It follows one under `*/**/*` or
  `src/**/*`.

  ### Decisions I made, and why
  1. **Second full walk instead of an intersection rule.** When git refuses the
  short walk, I walk again in full and judge as before. A submodule's folder is
  tracked, so it is never pruned, and git refuses the short walk exactly when it
  would refuse the full one. This keeps both old fallbacks exact: audits keep
  every file, discovery uses the root `.gitignore` only.
  2. **Only patterns that cannot follow a link are shortened** (a leading `**`
  and one name with no `/` or `\` and at most one `*`). Otherwise a hidden link
  inside an ignored folder would turn today's refusal into an answer. Every
  audit pattern and discovery's `**/*` qualify; include sets and globs like
  `src/**` are walked as before.
  3. **`./` and folders starting with `:` are never pruned**, because pruning
  them could hide the path that makes git refuse.
  4. **No pruning when git can't answer** (no git, not a repo, untrusted owner).
  For the audits the fallback keeps every file, so nothing can be pruned
  anyway. I left discovery's fallback as it is too, to keep one rule.
  5. **Untrusted owner is not simulated.** This container's global git config
  has `safe.directory=*`. The refusal is the same exit 128 as outside a
  repository, and that branch is tested.

› Message from general-purpose
  ## Leg 1: why a history rebuild is slow here, and what would make it fast

  I measured and changed no product code. The only code change is the test mend.
  Every run that loaded the machine went through the lane, and every summary I
  made was compared byte for byte with
  `/workspaces/Live-Documentation/.mdmd/history/b4294caf0e7d629f/`. All matched:
  60 of 60 summaries and 7,186 of 7,186 texts in every 60-commit run, 30 each
  in the two halves of the one-at-a-time run, and the single-commit runs too.

  ### What the processes wait for, and how I know
  1. **First, the history command's own process.** It writes every commit's tree
  on its one main thread. Each tree costs about 2.4 s of that thread on
  average, plus about 2.3 s of libuv's four threads, almost all of it system
  calls. The evidence:
     - Throughput stops improving above six processes: 3.6 s a commit at 6, 3.4
  at 10, 3.1 at 14.
     - The command's main thread is busy 69–75 % of each run, averaged over the
  whole run.
     - At 14 at a time a commit waits 18.4 s for a tree that takes 2–5 s on its
  own.
     - When I moved tree writing into small processes of their own (a probe
  option, `--tree-in-process`), that thread dropped to 9 % busy and the wait to
  10.9 s.
     - At 60 trees × ~2.4 s, the floor of the present design here is about 2.5 s
  a commit, roughly 55 minutes for the line, whatever the pool size.
  2. **Second, the processor cores: 20 logical processors are 10 cores.**
     - With the trees moved out, the same summaries cost 10.8 processor-seconds
  a commit alone and 29–31 at 14–20 processes. Little of that is waiting for a
  processor (0.5–8 s); the work itself runs slower on shared cores.
     - Ten processes pinned one per core (`taskset` to the even processors) gave
  3.03 s a commit. Fourteen spread over all 20 gave 2.92, and twenty gave 2.50.
  So the second thread of each core adds about a fifth of throughput, while
  each thread's work costs about 1.5× as much.
  3. **Ruled out, each by a run:**
     - **V8's background threads:** `--single-threaded` was only 2 % faster.
     - **The file system:** ext4 vs the `/tmp` overlay changed one head tree by
  4 % and eight at once by 12 %. A synchronous writer produced the same trees,
  file for file, with a quarter to a third of the processor time (measured at
  the early and middle commits; my probe's head figure is only a bound). So the
  writer's cost is its asynchronous handling of many small files, not the disk.
     - **The disk:** iowait was ≤ 7 s a run up to 14 processes. At 20 the disk
  was 36 % busy, because trees that live past the 30 s writeback reach the
  device; it is the next thing to watch.
     - **Memory:** 0.5–0.65 GB a process.
     - **git:** 1–2 processor-seconds a commit.
     - **Node 22's WebAssembly wait:** gone. Grammars load in 2–25 ms, and the
  head's index pass is idle 0.23 s of 3.53.

  ### The tables in short (all measured by me)

  **Throughput, 60-commit sample, built JavaScript, trees written by the
  command's process:**

  | Processes | s a commit |
  | --- | ---: |
  | 1 | 10.99 |
  | 2 | 6.93 |
  | 4 | 4.07 |
  | 6 | 3.58 |
  | 10 | 3.39 |
  | 14 | 3.12 |
  | 14 under tsx (today's command) | 3.18 |

  - Today's command therefore takes about **71 min for the line, plus 1.8 min of
  fixed cost on every run**.
  - Processor-seconds a commit (process user + system, then git, then the
  command's process) were 10.8 + 0.9 + 3.2 at 1 process and 25.3 + 1.9 + 4.8 at
  14.
  - Peak memory was 0.57–0.64 GB a process.

  **Experiments at 14 processes unless noted** (s a commit):

  | Run | s a commit |
  | --- | ---: |
  | trees moved into their own processes | 2.92 |
  | the same under tsx | 2.94 |
  | the same, 20 processes | 2.50 |
  | 10 pinned one per core | 3.03 |
  | `--single-threaded` | 2.86 |
  | trees on ext4 | 3.06 (another builder used 2.4 cores during it) |
  | **long-lived workers that write their own trees, 14** | **2.39** |
  | long-lived workers, 10 | 2.76 |

  - In the 14-worker run, each worker's first summary cost the same as a fresh
  process (17.6 vs 17.7 processor-seconds).
  - Every later summary was **a third cheaper**: 21.2 vs 32.4 processor-seconds
  for the same 46 commits.
  - Workers peaked at 435–530 MB after four to six summaries.

  **One commit alone** (wall / processor-seconds of the summarizing process):

  | Commit | Process | Tree |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `87b9e7b5` | 5.8 / 8.7 | 1.7 s |
  | `535ceefc` | 7.7 / 10.4 | 2.0 s |
  | head `21b6e602` | 12.1 / 15.0 (another run: 15.4 / 19.2) | 4.7 s |

  - Single runs vary by about ±25 %.
  - Module loading is 0.33–0.42 s for the built JavaScript and 1.2–1.5 s under
  tsx.
  - V8's worker threads take 2.9–5 processor-seconds a process.
  - At the head, `git check-ignore` takes 1.3 s and the main thread waits on it.
  - The text store, starting empty, takes 0.3–1.6 s.

  **Inside the passes** (main-thread CPU profile, sorted by what the work
  depends on):
  - **Work that depends only on one file's bytes** is 31–37 % of the main
  thread's busy time (1.4 / 2.4 / 4.3 s at the three commits). Most of it is the
  TypeScript parse, which runs twice for every TypeScript file (2.13 + 1.42 s
  at the head).
  - **Adapters, mixing extraction and resolution:** 5–11 %.
  - **Work that needs the rest of the tree:** 15–25 %.
  - **Writing the output:** 16–23 %.

  **Fixed cost:** about 105 s even with every summary cached. Of that:
  - ~30 s goes to reading every summary twice.
  - ~17 s goes to starting 1,333 git processes from a large process. The same
  diffs take 5.6 s from a small one; I believe the cost is the fork of the large
  heap, but did not trace it.
  - ~27 s goes to re-deriving and re-checking rows and shapes of steps already
  written.
  - 5–7 s is the head check.

  ### Ranked gains, each estimated for the whole line here
  1. **Long-lived workers that write their own trees**, with the git environment
  set for each task: about 47–51 min. Medium cost (worker protocol in
  `regenerate.ts` and `summarizeChange.ts`). The risks are the stale-state list
  below. Needs one rebuild.
  2. **A synchronous tree writer inside those workers:** about 42 min. Low risk;
  `git.test.ts` and the equivalence test guard it. Rides with the rebuild for
  1.
  3. **Cutting the fixed cost:** a warm run would go from about 2 min to under
  45 s (about 25 s if checking the cached summaries also folds into the resume).
  Read each summary once, ask git in one process, and resume the sequence from
  the last one written. No rebuild, because `computeHistory.ts` does not key the
  lens; only moving `changesBetween` within `git.ts` would. The resume's key is
  a design decision for you.
  4. **An in-memory memo, by content hash, of the bytes-only work:** about 33–36
  min. High cost and risk: the extraction/resolution seam does not exist yet.
  5. **Pool size and flags alone:** under 10 %. The present rule (processors −
  1, so 19 here and 3 on the runner) becomes right once trees leave the
  command's process.
  6. **Per-version results on disk:** last. It has the same ceiling as 4, and it
  does not help the rebuild a lens change causes.

  Smaller items:
  - Skipping `git check-ignore` in history trees: about 5 %, keyed.
  - tsx costs 1.6–2.1 processor-seconds a commit; long-lived workers pay it once
  each.

  **State that would carry from one commit to the next in a long-lived process**
  (from the reviewer subagent's read, two items checked by me):
  - **Inherited `GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` / `GIT_INDEX_FILE`:** read
  implicitly by `gitIgnored` and `standingFiles`. This would silently give wrong
  answers unless set per task.
  - **`rust.ts:595` `packageCache`:** stale if a path is ever reused.
  - **The tree-sitter parser map:** keeps a failed grammar load for the rest of
  the process.
  - **Six adapters' `factsCache` plus two folder caches:** grow by one path per
  commit.
  - **`maxRSS`** (`summarizeChange.ts:189`): measures the process's lifetime
  peak, not one commit's.
  - **pid-named temporary files:** collide only with two tasks at once in one
  process.

  ### The hosted runner

● The rebuild-speed measurements are in and on main, and a fresh builder is now

  What holds a rebuild back

  Every summary the builder made was checked byte for byte against the cache,
  and all matched.

  - Today's rebuild takes about 71 minutes for the 1,333 commits, plus about 1.8
    minutes of fixed cost on every run, even when nothing needs regenerating.
  - The first limit is one thread. The command's own process writes every
    commit's files to disk itself, on its one main thread, about 2.4 seconds per
    commit. So adding processes stops helping above six, whatever the pool's
    size.
  - The second limit is the cores: twenty threads are ten cores, and work on a
    shared core costs about half as much again.
  - My own guess was wrong. V8's background threads made a 2% difference. The
    disk, memory and git were also ruled out by runs. The slow start that Node
    22 had is gone under Node 26.
  - The fixed 1.8 minutes is every summary read and parsed twice, 1,333 git
    processes started one by one, and every already-written step re-derived and
    re-checked.

  What I've asked to be built

  The builder's own ranking ended at about 42 minutes, because it still treated
  each commit as a stranger. Successive commits share almost everything, so my
  design goes further:

  1. The fixed cost first. It needs no rebuild and lands by itself: a run with
     little to regenerate should cost seconds.
  2. Workers that live across commits and keep their files on disk, changing
     only what differs between one commit and the next. Writing those files is a
     quarter of all processor time today.
  3. Each file parsed once per version. Today every TypeScript file is parsed
     twice per commit, and 99% of those parses repeat a version already seen.
     This one comes back to me as a design with numbers before anything is
     built.

  Items 2 and 3 change code the history is keyed on. They stay on a branch
  behind an independent review, and are proved by one whole rebuild whose every
  summary must equal today's cache. The SQL, PowerShell and .NET readers then
  land on the faster rebuild.

  The danger in item 2, named by the measurements: a long-lived worker inherits
  git settings that point at its first commit's files, and would silently answer
  for the wrong commit unless they are set for every task. The brief names it
  and every other piece of state that could carry over.

    gate hold is behind the Playwright upgrade's whole-suite run, which has the
    lane now.
  - Out: the Playwright upgrade, the ignored-folder walk, and the rebuild
    speed-up.

  ### What was built (all in unkeyed files)
  1. **Each summary is read once, each text once.** The run's start now only
  checks that each summary file exists. Damage is found where the sequence reads
  a summary (`deriveSequence`): a summary that doesn't read, or the summary
  that first named a missing or changed text. A changed text is removed, that
  change is summarized again, and the sequence is read again. Texts are held to
  their hash once and kept for the words and the head check.
  2. **A run goes on from the sequence the last run wrote.** It writes a record
  beside the sequence, `<root>/history/history-resume.json`, after
  `history.json`. The record holds:
     - the SHA-256 of `history.json`, so it never describes another sequence;
     - the key: lens key, plus `sequenceCodeIdentity` (every non-test file of
  both packages, the lock, the version and Unicode, without the commit), plus
  the whole configuration;
     - the text hashes by id;
     - which change first named each text, so an old damaged text can be mended;
     - the entries each tree left out.

     A run goes on only if:
     - every commit of the written sequence equals today's first sampled commits
  as this run would write them (id, parents, date, author, subject);
     - the written sequence's last moment, replayed, equals its last summary
  read afresh.

     It then reads only that last summary plus the new ones, and still checks
  every new step's replay. `SequenceWriter.continuing` and
  `SequenceBuilder.continuing` were added in `sequence.ts`. `--rederive` forces
  the whole derivation.
  3. **The git words are asked early instead of from one process.**
  `changesBetween` is unchanged; it is now called for the new steps only, 8 at a
  time, before any summary is read, while the process heap is small. Asking one
  git process for all steps (`diff-tree --stdin`) would be new git code that
  must be proven equal to `git diff` at every pair. A continuing run asks only
  for its new steps, so I did not build that.
  4. **The head check reads from git's object store.** `committedLiveDocGraph`
  in `headCheck.ts` uses `ls-tree` plus one `cat-file --batch`, follows links
  with `followLink` (imported unchanged from `git.ts`), and parses each doc the
  way `readLiveDocGraph` does. It no longer writes the head's whole tree.

  ### Tests, and what I ran
  - **Tests run:** the history unit tests (18 files, 144 cases, green), `tsc`,
  `eslint`, and the new integration case alone (`history.test.ts -t "goes on
  from the sequence"`, about 30 s).
  - **Not yet run (in the gate hold):** the rest of the integration suite and

  - **The new unit test** in `sequence.test.ts` builds a sequence whole and in

  ### Decisions you should review
  - **One fault in the ruling's wording.** Only the whole written sequence can
  be reused, never just its first steps. A sequence that stops short of today's
  line holds strings in its tables, under ids, that a whole derivation would not
  have. So the rule I built is "every written commit is a prefix of today's
  line", plus the replay guard.
  - **The whole configuration is in the key**, not just the parts the reading
  uses (`bundleExclude` and the docs root). That is simpler and never wrong; the
  cost is one whole derivation after editing any other part of the
  configuration.
  - **A continuing run never reads old summaries**, so a damaged old summary is
  mended at the next whole derivation rather than at every run. Texts are still
  read and checked at every run, so a damaged text is mended at once.
  - **The head check now reads names as git stores them.** A doc name that a
  case-folding disk would have merged into another, or that the disk cannot
  hold, used to drop out; now it is read under its own name. The generator never
  writes such names.
  - **`headCheck.ts` now starts git**, so it joins `ACTING_UNKEYED` in
  `generatorIdentity.test.ts` with the reason "reads the committed docs for the
  check at the head, after every summary is made; nothing it reads reaches a
  summary". That list wants a reviewed reason, so this needs your review.
  - **`changesBetween` stays in `git.ts`.** If Milestone 2 changes `git.ts`
  anyway, moving the command's own git readings out of it is worth deciding
  then.

  What the first part does (the builder's account; I have read only its report):
  - A run with little to regenerate continues from the sequence the last run
    wrote, instead of re-deriving all 1,333 steps.
  - Each summary is read once instead of twice.

  When a run may continue from the written sequence. The builder corrected my
  ruling, and I accepted the correction: only the whole written sequence can be
  reused, never its first part. A run continues only when all of these hold;
  otherwise it derives everything, as today:
  - the same lens key, the same code and the same configuration;
  - every written commit matches today's line as far as it goes;
  - the written sequence's last moment replays to its last summary, read afresh.

  A flag forces the whole derivation.

  Two things I asked it to settle before it commits:
  - Uncommitted code edits must also force a whole derivation.
  - A run killed mid-write must lead to a whole derivation.

  The trade it makes, which the docs must state plainly: a continuing run does
  not re-read old summaries. A damaged one would be found at the next whole
  derivation, not at once. What is shown stays right meanwhile, because the
  written sequence is held to its own hash.

  ### Milestone 2, drafted in scratch only
  No keyed file is touched yet; that would move the lens under the queued runs.
  The drafts are in `/tmp/claude-1000/rf/m2/`:
  - **Tree writer split** (`git-forward.snippet.ts`): the writer becomes a plan
  (the listing's rules) plus a writing step. `bringTreeForward` then works like
  this:
    - It compares the new change's plan with what was actually written, not `git
  diff-tree`'s word. That makes links whose targets change, and excluded
  pictures written empty, come out right without extra rules.
    - It removes the docs root whole (the generator writes only there: docs,
  pruning, `index.json`).
    - It removes stale entries and the folders no entry needs.
    - It writes what is new, asking the disk first.
    - Wherever the disk refuses a name, or a folder that should be empty is not,
  it gives up and the tree is written anew. A case-folding disk could otherwise
  keep the later of two clashing names.
  - **Seam** (`repository.snippet.ts`): `WorkingTree.bringTo(change, directory)`
  and `broughtForward`. The tree's folder is renamed for every change, so no
  absolute path is ever reused. That deals with two stale-state items: the Rust
  adapter's folder cache (stale if a path is reused) and the per-path,
  modification-time caches of the other adapters.
  - **Worker** (`worker.snippet.ts`), running in `summarizeChange.ts`:
    - It clears the tree's git variables before each tree is written and sets
  them to that tree's before summarizing.
    - It sends warnings per task over the channel.
    - Its peak memory is the worker's own since it began, which is the figure a
  lane needs.
    - A worker is ended after any task where the generator failed a file,
  because a failed grammar load is kept in the process and would silently
  degrade its later commits.
  - **Pool** (`regenerate-pool.snippet.ts`): runs of consecutive commits, about
  four runs per worker, and a worker replaced every 100 tasks.
  - **Tests and driver:** a property test draft (`history-tree-forward.test.ts`)
  over the sample workspaces committed one after another with the generator run
  between steps, small edits of each kind, and this repository's commits near
  and far. The measuring driver is written:
  `history-rebuild-fast/worker-driver.cjs` in my worktree.

  ### Milestone 3, read only
  A subagent of my tier (Explore) found:
  - Nothing writes to a TypeScript syntax tree. The only writes are TypeScript's
  own lazy caches (`lineMap`, `modifierFlagsCache`), each a pure function of
  the tree and its text.
  - No reader uses `sourceFile.fileName`. The parse depends on the name only for
  `.d.ts`.
  - There are three parse sites: `sourceAnalysis.ts:91`, `discovery.ts:391` (not
  mine), and `dependencies.ts:548`. The last is a third parse of every `export
  *` target.
  - Memory figures and a design are still to come.

  ## Review of history-warm-run.patch (applied on 7d218b18d; SHA-256
  fc86eaacb6d2e507…, 16 files)

  The core claim holds. A run that goes on from the written sequence writes the
  same bytes a whole derivation writes, provided every input is the same. I
  found no way the join itself goes wrong. The faults are in what the go-on key
  is computed from, in the new head check, and in what the tests hold. Nine
  findings, most serious first. Line numbers are those after the patch.

  ### 1. The code identity is taken hours after the code was loaded
  (medium-high; shown by reading)
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:320`. `sequenceCodeIdentity()` is called while
  building `reading`, after `await summarize(missing)` (line 310). The lens
  identity, by contrast, is taken at line 218.
  - **What goes wrong:** the process loaded its reading code (codec, rows,
  derive, sequence) at start-up. If that code changes on disk during the run,
  the record is keyed with the new identity but holds what the old code wrote.
  - **Events:**
    1. A full rebuild starts with codec/derive version C1; regeneration takes
  hours.
    2. Meanwhile someone edits or commits an unkeyed reading module in the same
  checkout, say `rows.ts` `symbolRenames` or `directories.ts`.
    3. The run ends and writes `history-resume.json` with the key computed from
  the edited code, C2.
    4. The next run, under C2, has the same key and goes on.
    5. Steps 1..N stay C1's derivation and new steps are C2's.
  - **Why nothing catches it:** the join check compares only the last moment,
  and both rules replay to the same moments. The written sequence differs from
  what `--rederive` writes.
  - **Mend:** compute `sequenceCodeIdentity()` at line 218, beside
  `generatorIdentity()`, before any work.

  ### 2. The head check drops a doc reached through a second link (medium; shown
  by running `followLink`)
  - **Where:** `headCheck.ts:62–64, 69`. `targets` holds only the targets of
  links among the docs under the base layer. `followLink` needs the target of
  every link it meets on the way. The tree writer gives it all of them
  (`git.ts:414–416`).
  - **What goes wrong:** a doc that is a link to a link outside the base layer,
  or a link through a folder link, ends at "a symbolic link to nothing the
  commit holds". It is silently left out of the committed graph.
  - **Shown:** with both target maps on `.mdmd/layer-4/x/lens.ts.mdmd.md ->
  ../../layer-1/lens.ts.mdmd.md -> ../../real/…`, and on
  `.mdmd/layer-4/y.ts.mdmd.md -> ../shared/…` with `.mdmd/shared -> ../real`:
    - the tree writer's targets give `{"file":…}`;
    - the head check's targets give `{"reason":"it is a symbolic link to nothing
  the commit holds"}`.
  - **Consequence:** the old check read these docs. The new one fails the run
  with "X is in the history's last step and no doc of it is committed" and
  advises regenerating the mirror. No test covers this branch (mutation M2 below
  survived). The doc comment says "as the history's tree writer follows it"; it
  does not.
  - **Mend:** read the targets of every `120000` entry in `byPath`.

  ### 3. Nothing tests the go-on key, and for some changes it is the only guard
  (medium; shown by running a mutation)
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:860`.
  - **Why it matters:** the join check only sees differences visible at the last
  moment. Some changes alter earlier steps only:
    - a `bundleExclude` edit touching a file that existed only in early commits;
    - a change to `derive.ts` or `rows.ts` that reclassifies an earlier step
  (renamed versus gone-and-born) but replays to the same moments.
    For those, the key is the only guard.
  - **Mutations:** I applied three at once, ran `history.test.ts` and
  `history-reading.test.ts` through the machine's lane, and all 41 tests still
  passed. Files restored and the worktree checked byte-equal to the patch.
    - **M1:** deleted the key check.
    - **M2:** stopped following doc links in `committedLiveDocGraph`.
    - **M3:** attributed every damaged text to the last change instead of
  `firstNamed[id]`.
  - **Why M1 survives:** the only config-change test (history-reading's
  `bundleExclude` edit) is rescued by the join check falling back to a whole
  derivation, and it does not assert the reason line.
  - **Mend:** a test whose config or code change affects only an early commit,
  asserting a whole derivation and its reason.

  ### 4. The commit as handed is not ready (medium; shown by running)
  - **Mirror is stale:** `live-docs:generate --dry-run` over the history modules
  reports 4 docs to update. Missing from the generated sections:
    - `committedLiveDocGraph`, and headCheck's new dependencies;
    - `sequenceCodeIdentity` and `readsSummaries`;
    - the new sequence statics.
    With a stale mirror, this repository's own head check would fail at that
  commit.
  - **Broken links:** the docs, and the comment in `computeHistory.ts`, cite
  `AI-Agent-Workspace/AgentSessionHistory/2026/11/2026-11-19/Probes/history-rebu
  ild-fast/README.md`, which does not exist. `npm run slopcop:markdown` (part of
  `safe:commit`) exits 3 with 5 broken links.
  - **Trivial:** the header sentence "a run with nothing to regenerate took
  about 105 s before" gives no after figure.

  ### 5. The head check now fails where the summary itself left an entry out
  (low-medium; shown by reading)
  - **Where:** `headCheck.ts:42–48, 60–61`, and the headCheck doc, line 18.
  - **What changed:** the summary side still goes through the tree writer.
  Entries it leaves out are now read on the committed side only:
    - Windows-reserved names (`aux.ts`, `con.tsx`, `nul.js`, trailing dot or
  space);
    - case or normalization collisions on a folding disk;
    - names containing U+FFFD;
    - `.git`, `..` or empty path parts.
    In each case the head summary lacks the file, the committed graph has it,
  and the check fails with the "regenerate the mirror" remedy where the old
  check passed.
  - **The docs' claims:** "The generator writes no such names" is false; the
  generator mirrors source names. "the one a Windows disk needs" overstates it.
  - **Improved:** the other way round. ENAMETOOLONG on a doc path whose source
  still fits under Windows' path limit used to fail falsely and now passes.
  - **Mend:** hold the check against the head summary's own `unwritten` list:
  name those paths and exclude them, or fail giving that reason.

  ### 6. Mending a damaged text is only weakly tested (low; shown by mutation
  M3)
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:760`. The existing test damages texts the head
  change also names, so re-summarizing any change restores them.
  - **Risk:** a wrong attribution would turn "mends itself" into "fails every
  run".
  - **Mend:** a test that damages a text named only by the base commit.

  ### 7. Some damage makes every continuing run fail until `--rederive` (low;
  shown by reading)
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:338–348, 852–875`. The record itself is
  unprotected.
    - A record hash with a flipped hex digit names a text no re-summary writes.
  Every continuing run then throws "summarized again by this run and still do
  not read…" until `--rederive`, and the message never mentions `--rederive`.
    - A record file that is JSON `null` crashes `writtenSequence` with a
  TypeError.
    - Only texts in the last moment are cross-checked against the sequence.
  - **Mend:** on `still` during a continuation, retry once as a whole
  derivation. Check the record is an object. Optionally check
  `record.texts.length === sequence.words.texts`.

  ### 8. Git itself is not in the key (low; shown by reading)
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:736`, `git.ts:144`.
  - Steps already written keep git's rename and modified words from when they
  were written. A git upgrade (a container rebuild), or user git config beyond
  the pinned options, would change what a whole derivation writes.
  - **Mend:** add `git --version` to `continuationKey`.

  ### 9. Minor
  - `regenerated` and `cached` count a change twice when it was both missing and
  summarized again (lines 386–387).
  - `jobs` reports 1 when only damaged changes were redone.
  - `SequenceBuilder` now takes an arbitrary `writer` through its public
  constructor (`sequence.ts:157`); it could be kept internal.
  - `readBlobs` and the listing parse duplicate `git.ts`. That is justified,
  since editing `git.ts` moves the lens; fold them in at the next change that
  moves it anyway.
  - `sequenceCodeIdentity` repeats `checkoutOf`'s git calls.
  - Because the identity covers every non-test file of both packages, any engine
  or generator commit forces a whole derivation, including Pages runs. The
  saving is narrower than "the line only grew".

  ### What each kind of damage now does
  In a run that goes on, summaries before the last written change are never
  read.
  - **Truncated summary, wrong-lens summary, or one that no longer reads:**
    - before the join: never noticed in a continuing run, and `whole.json` still
  says the cache is whole. It is found at the next whole derivation:
  `--rederive`, any key change, a rewritten line, an authors toggle, or a
  missing or mismatched record.
    - at the join or after it: found at once and summarized again.
    - The sequence stays right meanwhile, unless such summaries legitimately
  differ under one key (a cache copied from another disk, whose `unwritten`
  differ). Then the continued sequence keeps the old reading.
  - **Changed or missing text:** found at once, since every text is read each
  run. It is removed and its first-naming change summarized again.
  - **Texts named only by files `bundleExclude` drops:** no longer checked (the
  old code checked them). They do not affect the sequence.

  ### Checked and found sound
  - **Bytes at the join:**
    - tables re-seeded in order; base, steps and keyframes carried;
    - keyframe encoding independent of Map order, since every string is already
  in the tables and tuples are sorted by unique ids;
    - rename targets can never collide, so the content after a step does not
  depend on order;
    - the builder's `previous` comes from the summary in both paths;
    - the join check covers every field the next step's derivation reads;
    - JSON round trip is identity, lone surrogates included.
  - **Prefix check:** catches a rewritten line, a deepened shallow clone, an
  authors toggle, and any sampling change that drops a written commit.
  - **Head and lens:** both are taken fresh each run.
  - **Kill orders:** at every point the record's hash forces a whole derivation
  or a consistent go-on. Overlapping runs: the lock holds, and even overlapping
  writers stay safe through the hash.
  - **The lens:**
    - With the patch applied, `generatorIdentity()` gives `modified:null`, and
  `keysTheLens` of every changed file is false. The key is unchanged.
    - `checkoutOf` filters exactly as before.
    - The `ACTING_UNKEYED` entry for `headCheck.ts` is justified by the code:
  only `computeHistory` imports it, it runs after every summary is made, and it
  writes nothing.
  - **Head check, regular cases:** for modes 100644/100755/120000/160000, LFS
  pointers, CRLF and links at or above the docs root, the new reading matches
  the old.
  - **Checks run:**
    - type-check of engine and generator: clean;
    - unit tests (sequence, window, words, generatorIdentity, computeHistory):
  43 passed;
    - `history.test.ts` and `generator-identity.test.ts` through the lane: 37
  passed.
  - **The new tests can fail:** `sequence.test.ts`'s two cases, the integration
  test's "continued equals unrecorded / `--rederive`" bytes, and the identity
  test each fail if what they hold breaks.

  ### Not checked
  - Windows or macOS behaviour, empirically.
  - A real repository's run time.
  - e2e, lint and the full gate.
  - Explorer consumers of the history folder.

  **Decisions for you to confirm:**
  - **The record now carries its own hash** (`check`), and its format is bumped
  to `live-docs-history-resume/2`. This goes beyond the ruling for finding 6. A

  ### What the mends bring

  **A. Low: the check at the head skips a whole file when only its doc was left
  out.** Shown by running the pure function.
  - **Where:** `headCheck.ts:142–148`, `leftOut.get(file.codePath) ??
  leftOut.get(file.docPath)`.
  - **What happens:** if the head's tree left out only the committed doc, every
  field of the file and every link to or from it is skipped. That includes
  symbols, dependencies and links the history did read from the source.
  - **Demonstration:** committed `src/a.ts` has a symbol, and the replayed rows
  have lost it.
    - `headDifferences` reports "the symbols of src/a.ts differ".
    - With `leftOut = {".mdmd/layer-4/src/a.ts.mdmd.md": …}` it reports nothing.
  The file is named in the line, but the check passes as applied.
  - **Why the branch adds nothing correct:** in realistic cases (a
  Windows-reserved name, a case or normalization collision, a non-UTF-8 name)
  the source and its doc are left out together, so the codePath branch already
  matches. The docPath branch only adds cover where it is too broad.
  - **The integration test leans on it:** it exercises only this branch. Its
  doc's content still names `src/cafe.ts`, a file the commit never holds, so a
  sound check would report that doc as stale.
  - **Mend:**
    - Drop the docPath branch, or, where only the doc was left out, compare
  everything but `authored`.
    - Make the integration test's doc carry the lossy codePath the generator
  would write, so it exercises the codePath branch.

  **B. Low, inherent: what the check skips now comes from the history's own
  record of what it left out.** Shown by reading.
  - The list is the head summary's own `unwritten`, the tree writer's report. A
  tree-writer fault that drops entries and reports them, like the link bug of
  2026-11-19, now passes the check, named. The first form of this change would
  have failed on it.
  - This is no weaker than the check before the whole change, which wrote the
  tree on both sides and dropped such entries from both silently.
  - **Mend:** none required; say so in `leftOutAtHead`'s notes. Optionally,
  report the check as skipped rather than applied when nothing remains to
  compare.

  **C. Low: the fallback's message can give the wrong reason.** Shown by
  reading.
  - **Where:** `computeHistory.ts:357–363`.
  - `wentOn` is also true when the summary at the join (`read(last)`) or a new
  step's summary keeps failing to read. The fallback then says "the record …
  still names texts they do not", which is not the cause.
  - The loop itself is bounded: `reading.rederive` stays set, so the fallback
  fires at most once, and the whole derivation then throws the right error.
  - **Mend:** word the message by what the damage was.

  **D. Trivia.**
  - **Hand-off through a module variable:** `sequence.ts` now passes the writer
  to the builder through a module-level variable. It is correct (set and
  consumed synchronously, cleared before anything can throw), but a private
  factory would say it more plainly.
  - **Dangling anchor:** `#the-independent-review-and-its-mends` does not exist
  in the probe README, and four docs link to it. The audit ignores fragments, so
  the gate passes.

  ### Checked and found sound
  - **None of the four mechanisms can make a run go on that should not:** the
  record's hash, the format raised to `/2`, the shape checks (`null`, arrays,
  field types) and git in the identity only add refusals.
  - **The fallback cannot loop or leave files a later run misreads:** it runs at
  most once per run, and writes a fresh record from a whole derivation; the
  test shows the next run goes on from it.
  - **Mismatched records:** a record of format 1, or one whose hash does not
  match, leads to one whole derivation.
  - **Skipped links are scoped:** only links whose ends are skipped files are
  filtered.
  - **Differences beside a skipped file still show:** a compared file's
  dependency on a skipped file is still compared, so it fails loudly rather than
  passing silently.
  - **Lens and counts:**
    - No lens-keyed file changed since 7d218b18d.
    - `regenerated` and `jobs` now count correctly.
    - Taking the two identities concurrently is safe: `git status` does not fail
  when it cannot take the index lock.
